items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "clock reaction".
items.answer: A reaction in which a sudden colour change after a measured time indicates that a fixed amount of product has formed
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a reaction in which a sudden colour change after a measured time indicates that a fixed amount of product has formed. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which change would NOT alter the gradient of a mass-loss graph for marble with excess acid?
options: using a larger volume of acid at the same concentration
items.answer: using a larger volume of acid at the same concentration
items.markingKey: D. Concentration unchanged.

items.stem: Distinguish between a discontinuous (sampling) method and a continuous method.
items.answer: In a continuous method a property (mass, volume, absorbance) is monitored throughout one run; in a sampling method portions are removed, quenched and analysed at intervals (e.g. by titration).
items.markingKey: In a continuous method a property (mass, volume, absorbance) is monitored throughout one run; in a sampling method portions are removed, quenched and analysed at intervals (e.g. by titration). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A tangent drawn to a concentration–time curve for a product at t = 0 passes through (0 s, 0.14 mol dm⁻³) and (50 s, 0.58 mol dm⁻³). What is the initial rate of reaction?
items.answer: 0.00880 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

items.stem: In a reaction, 48.0 cm³ of gas was collected in the first 30 s and 72.0 cm³ in the first 60 s. Calculate the mean rate in each 30 s interval and comment.
items.answer: 1.60 cm³ s⁻¹ then 0.800 cm³ s⁻¹: the rate halves as reactants are used up
items.markingKey: 1.60 cm³ s⁻¹ then 0.800 cm³ s⁻¹: the rate halves as reactants are used up

items.stem: A student follows the reaction of marble chips with excess hydrochloric acid by measuring mass loss. (a) Sketch the expected mass–time graph and explain its shape. (b) Explain how the initial rate can be found. (c) State and explain two changes that would increase the rate. (d) Suggest why the final mass loss is the same when powdered marble is used.
items.answer: (a) mass falls steeply at first then levels off: rate decreases as acid concentration and surface area fall; stops when CaCO₃ used up. (b) tangent at t = 0, gradient. (c) higher acid concentration/temperature/smaller chips – more frequent and/or more energetic collisions. (d) same amount of CaCO₃ → same mass of CO₂.
items.markingKey: (a) mass falls steeply at first then levels off: rate decreases as acid concentration and surface area fall; stops when CaCO₃ used up. (b) tangent at t = 0, gradient. (c) higher acid concentration/temperature/smaller chips – more frequent and/or more energetic collisions. (d) same amount of CaCO₃ → same mass of CO₂.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A reaction in which a sudden colour change after a measured time indicates that a fixed amount of product has formed"?
items.answer: clock reaction
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of clock reaction.

items.stem: Briefly explain why measuring the conductivity of a solution can be used to follow some reactions.
items.answer: If the number or type of ions changes during the reaction, the electrical conductivity changes in proportion to the extent of reaction.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If the number or type of ions changes during the reaction, the electrical conductivity changes in proportion to the extent of reaction. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Lukas writes: "The units of rate are always mol s⁻¹." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Rate in terms of concentration has units mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹; other units (cm³ s⁻¹, g s⁻¹) apply if volume or mass is measured.
items.markingKey: Rate in terms of concentration has units mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹; other units (cm³ s⁻¹, g s⁻¹) apply if volume or mass is measured. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the cotton wool plug is used when following a reaction by mass loss.
items.answer: It allows the gas to escape but prevents acid spray/droplets from leaving the flask, which would add to the mass loss.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It allows the gas to escape but prevents acid spray/droplets from leaving the flask, which would add to the mass loss. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The concentration of a reactant fell from 0.100 mol dm⁻³ to 0.0503 mol dm⁻³ in 20 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.
items.answer: 0.00249 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

items.stem: Which measurement is most suitable for following the rate of Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)?
options: absorbance (fading purple colour) in a colorimeter
absorbance of the solution in a colorimeter
volume of hydrogen collected in a gas syringe
items.answer: volume of hydrogen collected in a gas syringe
items.markingKey: D. The property that changes measurably here: volume of hydrogen collected in a gas syringe.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Initial rates are more useful than mean rates."
items.answer: Initial rates are essential for kinetic analysis, though mean rates are fine for simple comparisons.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: initial rate relates directly to known starting concentrations, so it is used to find orders; not affected by product build-up or reverse reaction. Arguments against: drawing a tangent introduces uncertainty; mean rates are easier to measure and adequate for comparisons. Supported judgement: Initial rates are essential for kinetic analysis, though mean rates are fine for simple comparisons. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
items.answer: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy.
items.markingKey: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy. More particles have E ≥ Ea(cat).

items.stem: Distinguish between a transition state and an intermediate.
items.answer: A transition state is an unstable arrangement at an energy maximum that cannot be isolated; an intermediate is a species formed in one step and used in a later step, at an energy minimum between peaks.
items.markingKey: A transition state is an unstable arrangement at an energy maximum that cannot be isolated; an intermediate is a species formed in one step and used in a later step, at an energy minimum between peaks. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why does a catalyst not change the enthalpy change of a reaction?
options: It is used up in the reaction.
It lowers the energy of the reactants.
It increases the energy of the products.
The energies of reactants and products are unchanged; only the pathway differs.
items.answer: The energies of reactants and products are unchanged; only the pathway differs.
items.markingKey: D. ΔH is a state function.

items.stem: Sketch a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution at two temperatures, T₁ < T₂, and use it to explain the effect of temperature on rate.
items.answer: T₂ curve flatter with peak at higher energy, same area; area beyond Ea larger at T₂ → more successful collisions
items.markingKey: T₂ curve flatter with peak at higher energy, same area; area beyond Ea larger at T₂ → more successful collisions

items.stem:
The initial rate of the hydrolysis of bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br + OH- → CH₃CH₂OH + Br-, was measured.

experiment | [CH₃CH₂Br] / mol dm⁻³ | [OH⁻] / mol dm⁻³ | initial rate / mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
1 | 0.0200 | 0.100 | 0.0179
2 | 0.0400 | 0.100 | 0.0358
3 | 0.0200 | 0.300 | 0.0537
4 | 0.0400 | 0.300 | 0.107

(a) Deduce the order of reaction with respect to CH₃CH₂Br and to OH⁻. [2]
(b) Write the rate equation and calculate the rate constant, including units. [3]
(c) Calculate the initial rate when [CH₃CH₂Br] = 0.0300 and [OH⁻] = 0.250 mol dm⁻³. [1]
(d) Use experiment 4 to check your rate equation. [1]
(e) State why the temperature must be kept constant in all experiments. [1]
items.answer: (a) 1 and 1 (b) rate = k[CH₃CH₂Br][OH⁻]; 8.95 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ (c) 0.0671 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (d) predicted 0.107, matches 0.107 (e) k depends on temperature, so a change would alter the rate independently of concentration.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Exps 1 and 2 → 1 (A1); exps 1 and 3 → 1 (A1). (b) [3] rate = k[CH₃CH₂Br][OH⁻] (A1); k = 8.95 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ (A1, units A1). (c) [1] rate = k × 0.0300 × 0.250 = 0.0671 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (A1). (d) [1] Predicted rate equals measured rate (1). (e) [1] k varies with T (1).

items.stem: Using f = e^(−Ea/RT), determine the ratio f(298 K)/f(288 K) for a reaction with activation energy 90 kJ mol⁻¹, and comment on the effect of temperature on rate.
items.markingKey: D. ratio = exp[(Ea/R)(1/288 − 1/298)] = exp[90000/8.31 × (1.17 × 10⁻⁴)] (M1) = 3.53 (A1); a small rise in T greatly increases the fraction of successful collisions (R1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Catalysts are the single most important factor in making industrial processes sustainable."
items.answer: Catalysts are vital for sustainability, but they work together with renewable feedstocks, energy efficiency and recycling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: allow lower temperatures and pressures, saving energy; improve selectivity, reducing waste; enable greener routes (enzymes, zeolites). Arguments against: many catalysts use scarce or toxic metals (Pt, Pd, Rh); feedstock choice, energy source and recycling are equally important; catalysts can be poisoned and need replacing. Supported judgement: Catalysts are vital for sustainability, but they work together with renewable feedstocks, energy efficiency and recycling.

items.stem:
The rate constant of a reaction was measured at several temperatures.

T / K | k / s⁻¹ | (1/T) / 10⁻³ K⁻¹ | ln k
293 | 8.97 × 10⁻⁵ | 3.413 | −9.32
303 | 3.01 × 10⁻⁴ | 3.300 | −8.11
313 | 9.33 × 10⁻⁴ | 3.195 | −6.98
323 | 0.00270 | 3.096 | −5.91
333 | 0.00733 | 3.003 | −4.92

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line, and explain why. [2]
(b) Determine the gradient of the line using the first and last points. [2]
(c) Calculate the activation energy. [1]
(d) Determine the frequency factor, A. [2]
(e) Suggest why using a line of best fit through all points is better than using two points. [1]
items.answer: (a) ln k (y) against 1/T (x), because ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T). (b) −10700 K (c) 89.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (d) 7.46 × 10¹¹ s⁻¹ (e) It uses all the data, reducing the effect of random error in any single measurement.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] ln k vs 1/T (1); linear form of Arrhenius equation (1). (b) [2] (−4.92 − −9.32)/(3.003 − 3.413) × 10³ (M1) = −10700 K (A1). (c) [1] Ea = −gradient × R = 10700 × 8.31 = 89.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1). (d) [2] ln A = ln k − gradient/T = 27.34 (M1); A = 7.46 × 10¹¹ s⁻¹ (A1). (e) [1] Averages random errors / identifies outliers (1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "heterogeneous catalyst".
items.answer: A catalyst in a different phase from the reactants, e.g. solid iron in the Haber process
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a catalyst in a different phase from the reactants, e.g. solid iron in the Haber process. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "heterogeneous catalyst"?
options: The power to which the concentration of a reactant is raised in the rate equation
The number of particles (molecules, atoms or ions) that take part in an elementary step
A catalyst in a different phase from the reactants, e.g. solid iron in the Haber process
A straight line touching a curve at one point; its gradient gives the instantaneous rate at that time
items.answer: A catalyst in a different phase from the reactants, e.g. solid iron in the Haber process
items.markingKey: C. "heterogeneous catalyst" is a catalyst in a different phase from the reactants, e.g. solid iron in the Haber process.

items.stem: Explain why powdered zinc reacts faster with acid than a lump of zinc of the same mass.
items.answer: The powder has a much larger surface area, so more zinc atoms are exposed to collisions with H⁺ ions per unit time.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The powder has a much larger surface area, so more zinc atoms are exposed to collisions with H⁺ ions per unit time. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Increasing temperature lowers the activation energy." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Ea is (approximately) constant; more particles have energy greater than or equal to it at higher temperature.
items.markingKey: Ea is (approximately) constant; more particles have energy greater than or equal to it at higher temperature. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An energy profile shows a forward activation energy of 105 kJ mol⁻¹ and an enthalpy change of +76 kJ mol⁻¹. Determine Ea for the reverse reaction.
items.answer: 29 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: C. Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH = 105 − (+76) = 29 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.stem: When ethene reacts with hydrogen over nickel, the rate increases if the temperature is increased. What is the best explanation?
options: more frequent collisions and a greater proportion with E ≥ Ea
the enthalpy change becomes more negative
larger surface area, so more frequent collisions
an alternative pathway with lower Ea, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful
items.answer: more frequent collisions and a greater proportion with E ≥ Ea
items.markingKey: A. the temperature is increased → more frequent collisions and a greater proportion with E ≥ Ea.

items.stem: The fraction of collisions with energy ≥ Ea is approximately e^(−Ea/RT). For Ea = 75 kJ mol⁻¹, calculate by what factor this fraction increases when the temperature rises from 310 K to 340 K.
items.markingKey: ratio = exp[(Ea/R)(1/310 − 1/340)] = exp[75000/8.31 × (2.85 × 10⁻⁴)] (M1) = 13.1 (A1); a small rise in T greatly increases the fraction of successful collisions (R1).

items.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly at room temperature but rapidly when manganese(IV) oxide is added. (a) Write an equation for the decomposition. (b) Draw an energy profile for the catalysed and uncatalysed reactions (ΔH = −98 kJ mol⁻¹). (c) Explain the effect of the catalyst using a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. (d) Describe how you would show that MnO₂ is not used up.
items.answer: (a) 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. (b) exothermic profile, catalysed peak lower, same ΔH. (c) lower Ea line; larger area beyond it; more successful collisions. (d) filter, wash, dry and weigh the MnO₂ before and after; same mass; reuse to show it still catalyses.
items.markingKey: (a) 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. (b) exothermic profile, catalysed peak lower, same ΔH. (c) lower Ea line; larger area beyond it; more successful collisions. (d) filter, wash, dry and weigh the MnO₂ before and after; same mass; reuse to show it still catalyses.

items.stem:
Magnesium ribbon was added to excess hydrochloric acid and the hydrogen produced was collected in a gas syringe (uncertainty ±0.5 cm³). Room conditions: 298 K, 100 kPa.

time / s | volume of H₂ / cm³
0 | 0.0
30 | 41.7
60 | 64.3
90 | 76.6
120 | 83.2
150 | 86.8
180 | 88.7

(a) Calculate the mean rate of hydrogen production in the first 30 s and between 90 s and 120 s. [2]
(b) Explain the difference between the two rates. [2]
(c) Calculate the amount of hydrogen collected after 180 s, using pV = nRT. [2]
(d) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the volume reading at 30 s. [1]
(e) State how the initial rate could be determined more accurately from these data. [1]
items.answer: (a) 1.39 and 0.220 cm³ s⁻¹ (b) The acid concentration and the magnesium surface area decrease as the reaction proceeds, so collisions become less frequent. (c) 0.00358 mol (d) 1.2 % (e) Plot volume against time and draw a tangent to the curve at t = 0; calculate its gradient.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] 41.7/30 = 1.39 cm³ s⁻¹ (A1); (83.2 − 76.6)/30 = 0.220 cm³ s⁻¹ (A1). (b) [2] Reactants used up / lower concentration (1); fewer collisions per unit time (1). (c) [2] n = pV/RT = 1.00 × 10⁵ × 88.7 × 10⁻⁶ / (8.31 × 298) (M1) = 0.00358 mol (A1). (d) [1] 0.5/41.7 × 100 = 1.2 % (A1). (e) [1] Tangent at t = 0 on a plotted curve (1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "rate equation".
items.answer: An experimentally determined expression rate = k[A]^m[B]^n relating the rate to the concentrations of reactants
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an experimentally determined expression rate = k[A]^m[B]^n relating the rate to the concentrations of reactants. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between the rate constant and the rate of reaction.
items.answer: The rate changes as concentrations change during a reaction; the rate constant k is fixed at a given temperature.
items.markingKey: The rate changes as concentrations change during a reaction; the rate constant k is fixed at a given temperature. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the iodination of propanone is zero order with respect to iodine.
items.answer: Iodine is not involved in the rate-determining step (enol formation, catalysed by H⁺); it reacts in a fast later step. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Iodine is not involved in the rate-determining step (enol formation, catalysed by H⁺); it reacts in a fast later step. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

experiment | [H₂O₂] / mol dm⁻³ | [I⁻] / mol dm⁻³ | initial rate / mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

items.answer: 1 in H₂O₂, 1 in I⁻; rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻]; k = 0.714 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

items.stem: The rate equation for the reaction of bromate(V) and bromide ions in excess acid is rate = k[BrO₃⁻][Br⁻]. What are the units of k?
items.answer: dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
items.markingKey: B. overall order 2 → k = rate/(conc)² → dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The initial-rates method is the best way to determine orders of reaction."
items.answer: Initial rates are reliable and widely used, but half-life and graphical methods can be more efficient.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: each experiment isolates one reactant; avoids complications from products and reverse reactions. Arguments against: requires several experiments and tangent drawing (uncertainty); continuous monitoring with half-life analysis can give the order from one run; isolation (large excess) methods may be simpler. Supported judgement: Initial rates are reliable and widely used, but half-life and graphical methods can be more efficient.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "half-life"?
options: The time taken for the concentration of a reactant to fall to half its initial value
The change in concentration (or amount) of a reactant or product per unit time
A species formed in one step of a mechanism and consumed in a later step
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway of lower activation energy, and is unchanged chemically at the end
items.answer: The time taken for the concentration of a reactant to fall to half its initial value
items.markingKey: A. "half-life" is the time taken for the concentration of a reactant to fall to half its initial value.

items.stem: What happens to the half-life of a first-order reaction if the initial concentration is doubled?
items.answer: It stays the same.
items.markingKey: C. t½ = ln 2/k.

items.stem: Rafael writes: "The orders in the rate equation are the coefficients in the balanced equation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Orders are found by experiment and relate to the rate-determining step; e.g. 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂ is first order.
items.markingKey: Orders are found by experiment and relate to the rate-determining step; e.g. 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂ is first order. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a proposed mechanism can be shown to be wrong but never proved correct by kinetic data.
items.answer: A mechanism must agree with the rate equation and the overall equation; several different mechanisms can fit the same data, so agreement supports but does not prove it.

items.stem: Distinguish between a catalyst in a mechanism and an intermediate.
items.answer: An intermediate is formed then consumed; a catalyst is consumed in an early step and regenerated later.
items.markingKey: An intermediate is formed then consumed; a catalyst is consumed in an early step and regenerated later. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The proposed mechanism for 2NO₂ + F₂ → 2NO₂F is: Step 1 (slow): NO₂ + F₂ → NO₂F + F; Step 2 (fast): NO₂ + F → NO₂F. Which rate equation is consistent with this mechanism?
items.answer: rate = k[NO₂][F₂]
items.markingKey: B. The slow step (and any fast equilibrium before it) determines the rate: rate = k[NO₂][F₂].

items.stem:
The rate constant of a reaction was measured at several temperatures.

T / K | k / s⁻¹ | (1/T) / 10⁻³ K⁻¹ | ln k
293 | 4.68 × 10⁻⁶ | 3.413 | −12.27
303 | 1.66 × 10⁻⁵ | 3.300 | −11.01
313 | 5.41 × 10⁻⁵ | 3.195 | −9.82
323 | 1.64 × 10⁻⁴ | 3.096 | −8.72
333 | 4.66 × 10⁻⁴ | 3.003 | −7.67

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line, and explain why. [2]
(b) Determine the gradient of the line using the first and last points. [2]
(c) Calculate the activation energy. [1]
(d) Determine the frequency factor, A. [2]
(e) Suggest why using a line of best fit through all points is better than using two points. [1]
items.answer: (a) ln k (y) against 1/T (x), because ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T). (b) −11200 K (c) 93.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (d) 2.02 × 10¹¹ s⁻¹ (e) It uses all the data, reducing the effect of random error in any single measurement.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] ln k vs 1/T (1); linear form of Arrhenius equation (1). (b) [2] (−7.67 − −12.27)/(3.003 − 3.413) × 10³ (M1) = −11200 K (A1). (c) [1] Ea = −gradient × R = 11200 × 8.31 = 93.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1). (d) [2] ln A = ln k − gradient/T = 26.03 (M1); A = 2.02 × 10¹¹ s⁻¹ (A1). (e) [1] Averages random errors / identifies outliers (1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Kinetic data are the best evidence for a reaction mechanism."
items.answer: Kinetics is a key test, but mechanisms are best supported by several independent lines of evidence.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rate equations directly test which species are in the RDS; orders rule out many mechanisms. Arguments against: several mechanisms may fit the same rate equation; isotopic labelling, stereochemistry and detection of intermediates give independent evidence. Supported judgement: Kinetics is a key test, but mechanisms are best supported by several independent lines of evidence.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "rate-determining step"?
options: The constant of proportionality k in the rate equation; it depends on temperature but not on concentration
The slowest step in a reaction mechanism, which determines the overall rate
The rate of reaction at time zero, found from the gradient of the tangent to the concentration–time curve at t = 0
The highest-energy arrangement of atoms along the reaction pathway, at the peak of the energy profile
items.answer: The slowest step in a reaction mechanism, which determines the overall rate
items.markingKey: B. "rate-determining step" is the slowest step in a reaction mechanism, which determines the overall rate.

items.stem: A mechanism has a fast equilibrium before a slow step. Which species appear in the rate equation?
options: only those in the fast step
only those in the slow step
all species in the overall equation
those in the slow step, with any intermediate replaced by the reactants that formed it
items.answer: those in the slow step, with any intermediate replaced by the reactants that formed it
items.markingKey: D. Pre-equilibrium.

items.stem: A student claims: "The slow step is always the first step of a mechanism." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The rate-determining step can be any step; if a fast pre-equilibrium comes first, reactants in it also appear in the rate equation.
items.markingKey: The rate-determining step can be any step; if a fast pre-equilibrium comes first, reactants in it also appear in the rate equation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An Arrhenius plot has a gradient of −6500 K. Calculate the activation energy.
An Arrhenius plot (ln k vs 1/T) has a gradient of −11 000 K. Determine Ea.
items.answer: 91.4 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: A. Ea = −gradient × R = 11000 × 8.31 = 91400 J mol⁻¹ = 91.4 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.stem: The rate constant of a reaction is 6.46 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ at 303 K and 0.0329 s⁻¹ at 343 K. Calculate the activation energy.
items.answer: 84.9 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: The reaction 2NO(g) + 2H₂(g) → N₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) has rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. (a) State the overall order. (b) Propose a two-step mechanism consistent with the rate equation and identify the intermediate. (c) The rate constant doubles when the temperature rises from 1100 K to 1150 K. Calculate Ea. (d) Explain why the reaction is very slow at room temperature.
items.answer: (a) 3. (b) 2NO + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O₂ (slow); H₂O₂ + H₂ → 2H₂O (fast); intermediate H₂O₂ (or N₂O pathway). (c) ln 2 = (Ea/8.31)(1/1100 − 1/1150) → Ea ≈ 146 kJ mol⁻¹. (d) high Ea: very small fraction of collisions have E ≥ Ea at 298 K.
items.markingKey: (a) 3. (b) 2NO + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O₂ (slow); H₂O₂ + H₂ → 2H₂O (fast); intermediate H₂O₂ (or N₂O pathway). (c) ln 2 = (Ea/8.31)(1/1100 − 1/1150) → Ea ≈ 146 kJ mol⁻¹. (d) high Ea: very small fraction of collisions have E ≥ Ea at 298 K.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A catalyst in the same phase as the reactants, e.g. H⁺(aq) in esterification"?
items.answer: homogeneous catalyst
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of homogeneous catalyst.

items.stem: What shape is a graph of rate against concentration for a zero-order reactant?
options: a straight line through the origin
items.answer: a horizontal straight line
items.markingKey: B. rate independent of [A].

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "rate of reaction"?
options: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway of lower activation energy, and is unchanged chemically at the end
An experimentally determined expression rate = k[A]^m[B]^n relating the rate to the concentrations of reactants
The change in concentration (or amount) of a reactant or product per unit time
The number of particles (molecules, atoms or ions) that take part in an elementary step
items.answer: The change in concentration (or amount) of a reactant or product per unit time
items.markingKey: C. "rate of reaction" is the change in concentration (or amount) of a reactant or product per unit time.

items.stem: Why can the rate equation not be deduced from the overall balanced equation?
options: The balanced equation is never correct.
The equation does not show the catalyst.
The rate depends on the mechanism, in particular the rate-determining step.
items.answer: The rate depends on the mechanism, in particular the rate-determining step.
items.markingKey: D. Kinetics ≠ stoichiometry.

items.stem: Explain why not all collisions between reactant particles lead to a reaction.
items.answer: Particles must collide with energy at least equal to the activation energy and with the correct orientation (geometry) so that bonds can break and form.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Particles must collide with energy at least equal to the activation energy and with the correct orientation (geometry) so that bonds can break and form. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The rate constant increases as the reaction proceeds." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: k is constant at constant temperature; the rate falls because concentrations fall.
items.markingKey: k is constant at constant temperature; the rate falls because concentrations fall. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why does the volume of gas collected per minute decrease as the reaction proceeds?
options: The concentration of the reactants decreases.
items.answer: The concentration of the reactants decreases.
items.markingKey: C. Lower concentration → fewer collisions.

items.stem: Distinguish between an intermediate and a catalyst in a mechanism.
items.answer: An intermediate is formed then consumed; a catalyst is consumed in an early step and regenerated later.
items.markingKey: An intermediate is formed then consumed; a catalyst is consumed in an early step and regenerated later. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a heterogeneous catalyst and a homogeneous catalyst.
items.answer: A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants (often forming an intermediate); a heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase and works by adsorption on its surface.
items.markingKey: A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants (often forming an intermediate); a heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase and works by adsorption on its surface. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: For the oxidation of nitrogen monoxide, rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. By what factor does the rate change if [NO] is tripled and [O₂] is halved?
items.markingKey: B. factor = (3)² × (½) = 4.5.

items.stem: The concentration of a reactant fell from 0.100 mol dm⁻³ to 0.0759 mol dm⁻³ in 40 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.
items.answer: 6.03 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

items.stem: A reaction has Ea = 68 kJ mol⁻¹ and k = 1.67 × 10⁻⁴ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ at 310 K. Calculate k at 360 K.
items.answer: 0.00651 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

items.stem: When calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid, the rate increases if a catalyst is added. What is the best explanation?
options: the enthalpy change becomes more negative
larger surface area, so more frequent collisions
more particles per unit volume, so more frequent collisions
an alternative pathway with lower Ea, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful
items.answer: an alternative pathway with lower Ea, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful
items.markingKey: D. a catalyst is added → an alternative pathway with lower Ea, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.

items.stem: In the acid hydrolysis of sucrose (first order), the half-life is 20 s. Starting from [C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁] = 1.20 mol dm⁻³, calculate the concentration after 40 s and the rate constant.

Magnesium ribbon was added to excess hydrochloric acid and the hydrogen produced was collected in a gas syringe (uncertainty ±0.5 cm³). Room conditions: 298 K, 100 kPa.

time / s | volume of H₂ / cm³
0 | 0.0
30 | 41.6
60 | 56.6
90 | 62.0
120 | 63.9
150 | 64.6
180 | 64.9

(a) Calculate the mean rate of hydrogen production in the first 30 s and between 90 s and 120 s. [2]
(b) Explain the difference between the two rates. [2]
(c) Calculate the amount of hydrogen collected after 180 s, using pV = nRT. [2]
(d) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the volume reading at 30 s. [1]
(e) State how the initial rate could be determined more accurately from these data. [1]

(c) [2] n = pV/RT = 1.00 × 10⁵ × 64.9 × 10⁻⁶ / (8.31 × 298) (M1) = 0.00262 mol (A1). (d) [1] 0.5/41.6 × 100 = 1.2 % (A1). (e) [1] Tangent at t = 0 on a plotted curve (1).

items.stem: A reaction has Ea = 90 kJ mol⁻¹ and k = 0.0458 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ at 300 K. Calculate k at 310 K.
items.answer: 0.147 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

items.stem: "The initial-rates method is the best way to determine orders of reaction." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Initial rates are reliable and widely used, but half-life and graphical methods can be more efficient.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: each experiment isolates one reactant; avoids complications from products and reverse reactions. Arguments against: requires several experiments and tangent drawing (uncertainty); continuous monitoring with half-life analysis can give the order from one run; isolation (large excess) methods may be simpler. Supported judgement: Initial rates are reliable and widely used, but half-life and graphical methods can be more efficient. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Which statement about a catalysed reaction is correct?
items.answer: ΔH is unchanged.
items.markingKey: B. Only the pathway changes.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The power to which the concentration of a reactant is raised in the rate equation"?
items.answer: order of reaction
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of order of reaction.

items.stem: How is the initial rate found from a graph of product concentration against time?
items.answer: from the gradient of the tangent at t = 0
items.markingKey: from the gradient of the tangent at t = 0. Instantaneous rate at t = 0.

items.stem: Explain how a graph of ln k against 1/T is used to determine the activation energy.
items.answer: ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T), so a plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with gradient −Ea/R; Ea = −gradient × R.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T), so a plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with gradient −Ea/R; Ea = −gradient × R. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: How does an enzyme act as a catalyst?
options: It raises the temperature of the cell.
It changes ΔH of the reaction.
It shifts equilibria to the right.
Its active site binds the substrate, providing a pathway of lower activation energy.
items.answer: Its active site binds the substrate, providing a pathway of lower activation energy.
items.markingKey: D. Biological catalyst.

items.stem: Explain why orders of reaction must be determined experimentally.
items.answer: Orders depend on the mechanism (the rate-determining step), which cannot be deduced from the stoichiometric equation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Orders depend on the mechanism (the rate-determining step), which cannot be deduced from the stoichiometric equation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a continuous method and a discontinuous (sampling) method.
items.answer: In a continuous method a property (mass, volume, absorbance) is monitored throughout one run; in a sampling method portions are removed, quenched and analysed at intervals (e.g. by titration).
items.markingKey: In a continuous method a property (mass, volume, absorbance) is monitored throughout one run; in a sampling method portions are removed, quenched and analysed at intervals (e.g. by titration). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: How does a catalyst change an Arrhenius plot?
options: The line is less steep because Ea is lower.
items.answer: The line is less steep because Ea is lower.
items.markingKey: B. Gradient = −Ea/R.

items.stem: Distinguish between the effect of temperature on rate and the effect of a catalyst on rate.
items.answer: Raising temperature increases particle energies so more exceed the same Ea; a catalyst leaves the energies unchanged but lowers Ea.
items.markingKey: Raising temperature increases particle energies so more exceed the same Ea; a catalyst leaves the energies unchanged but lowers Ea. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Measuring the volume of gas produced is the best way to follow the rate of any reaction." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: It is convenient for gas-producing reactions, but the best method depends on which property changes measurably.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: continuous, simple and gives many data points; precise gas syringes are available. Arguments against: only works when a gas is produced; soluble gases (CO₂, NH₃) give low readings; colorimetry or conductivity may be more precise and do not disturb the system. Supported judgement: It is convenient for gas-producing reactions, but the best method depends on which property changes measurably. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: "The Arrhenius equation shows that temperature is the most important factor affecting rate." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Temperature has a powerful exponential effect, but catalysts and conditions are often more practical levers.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: k depends exponentially on T; small T changes cause large rate changes. Supported judgement: Temperature has a powerful exponential effect, but catalysts and conditions are often more practical levers.
